commentary.bottom_line: Eight studies, two in real deployment, found that re-testing after updates, prompt changes, or compression detected both gains and regressions, including an 11.96% accuracy drop in a mammography model. No study compared re-testing with no re-testing or measured patient harm, so the evidence shows that re-testing detects change rather than that it prevents harm.

perspectives.view: Eight studies test re-testing after changes, and all report that it detected performance shifts. Two are prospective real-deployment studies; six are offline replays, vignettes, or benchmarks. None compares re-testing with no re-testing or measures patient harm. Certainty is low because outcomes are indirect and samples are small or simulated.

Repeat testing after a mammography model update found accuracy of 0.81 against a declared 0.92. Another software update raised AUC from 0.76 to 0.78 but cut specificity at the old threshold from 45.8% to 23.1%. A note-pipeline change raised major hallucinations from 4 to 25. Updates may improve one metric while degrading another.

In an ICU note study, a model upgrade raised accuracy from 69.12% to 80.3% while commission errors rose from 1.30% to 3.92%. Prompt edits also act as changes, and four prompt optimizations on one agent produced 18 to 28 point regressions. Re-testing may need to cover prompts, retrieval, and thresholds and to report error types.

Every compression method in an ICU prediction benchmark shifted subgroup AUROC by 1 to 4 points, which suggests re-testing should report results by subgroup. One test included older adults in Viet Nam. No test enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, so detection of regressions in these groups is untested.

FDA change control plan guidance asks whether modifications follow prespecified methods and performance specifications, and NIST AI 600-1 calls for reassessment after fine-tuning or retrieval changes. Vendor updates to general models sit outside device pathways; one study found a refusal safeguard lapsed within 12 weeks, and 21.5% of appropriate responses became inappropriate after updates.

Repeat calibration testing ran in a program covering 404,502 mammograms, though no study reported staff time or cost. Benchmark data may help set testing depth by change type, since INT8 quantization shifted accuracy by at most 1.9% while INT4 reduced one model's MedMCQA score by 19.7%. Successive call-handling iterations were evaluated across 307,000 calls.

Patients using public chatbots may not know when the underlying model changes. One model that initially refused to produce health disinformation no longer refused 12 weeks later, and fine-tuning another model on vaccination data raised safety concerns by 400%. No test of re-testing reported patient-facing outcomes such as trust or access to a human.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares deployments that re-test after changes with those that do not, and none links re-testing to patient harm, near misses, or clinician workload. Studies also do not report the cost or staffing needed to re-test at each update, do not examine vendor-pushed updates to general-purpose models under health-system re-testing, and do not test whether re-testing restores thresholds calibrated for earlier versions.
commentary.underserved_note: Only one test named a population of interest, older adults in Viet Nam, and none included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups cannot assume that re-testing results from other settings capture regressions their patients would face, and the subgroup shifts seen after compression suggest local re-testing stratified by population may be needed.
